0: Have you ever run into this: a model is excellent at writing code and doing maths, but when you ask it an everyday question it answers nonsense.
1: We all know that to improve a particular capability while a model is training, you look for data of that kind specifically,
2: But a lot of that data is hard to find by searching the internet directly. A single entry point for downloading data saves model trainers a great deal of effort.
3: For example, the Chinese dataset we open-sourced, distilled from full DeepSeek-R1: much of its raw data was downloaded straight from ModelScope,
4: Fine-tuning our model can start from a ready-made open dataset, which lets us get the whole pipeline working quickly.
6: ModelScope brings together more than 40,000 open datasets. The platform supports dataset search and preview, and provides field descriptions and dataset versions.
7: ModelScope lets you search datasets by keyword tags and task category, for example to find Chinese binary text-classification data.
9: Once you have filtered the datasets, pick the one you are interested in and click “Data preview” to inspect sample content and field descriptions online, which helps you decide. Take simpleai/HC3-Chinese as an example.
10: Which column holds the question, which holds the answer, whether there are labels, whether one record is a paragraph or a set of turns — you can see all of that first. Later, when you write the processing code, you will not have to guess from field names.
11: Take question-answering data: human answers and model answers may sit in different fields. Which task you are preparing it for decides which fields to read and how to arrange them — you cannot just see the words question and answer and start training.
12: Then look at the files and versions of the dataset. The same dataset gets updated, and the training samples, fields or splits can change too. Note which version you used in an experiment, and reproducing it later becomes much easier.
13: The dataset description and licence are worth reading alongside. Data you can download may come with different requirements for research, training or commercial products.
15: ModelScope provides the MsDataset.load interface for loading datasets in Python. Once ModelScope is installed, you can follow the instructions on the dataset page.

19: Some datasets keep data from different sources, domains or purposes apart. If you care about only one part, use subset_name to name the subset.
20: For example, reading the baike subset inside HC3-Chinese.
21: When you switch to another dataset, check which subsets it has first. baike is the specific name here and cannot be reused as-is on another dataset.
23: A subset picks which kind of data; split picks which division of the data. The common ones are the training set train, the validation set validation and the test set test.
24: To read only the training split of the baike subset, add one more argument.
25: Not every dataset provides all three splits; check the dataset description for the exact names. Once you have the training set, print one sample first to confirm the fields and content are as expected before wiring in the rest of the processing code.
27: After data is updated, the same code may read different content. Taking version v1 of HC3-Chinese as an example, you can specify it explicitly with version.
28: In practice, check the dataset page for the available versions. If a version keeps being updated, also keep the data files or checksums you used at the time, so you can compare later.
30: First draw a few samples to check for empty values, garbled text or obvious errors, then confirm the fields meet what the training code expects. If the answer format for the same batch of questions varies a lot, that needs tidying up first.
31: Training data and test data also need separating. Do not mix the samples you plan to use for checking model quality into the training set in advance — otherwise the score looks good, but it is hard to tell how the model handles new questions.
